title: Nothing on our own
hook: on our own we can do nothing; all happens in His color (Sukhmani 15)

segments.voice: Yesterday, birthaa: the One full of every power also knows every heart's pain. Today the fifteenth ashtpadi gives everything we do a color.

In old Punjab, cloth was dyed by hand. You'd soak plain white cotton in a vat, and when you lifted it out, it had become saffron, or indigo, or deep red. A good dye doesn't sit on top of the cloth like paint. It goes into every thread. You can't scrape it off. The cloth is still cloth, but every part of it carries the color. Gurbani returns to that picture, and today it's the way into a hard teaching: nothing on our own.
screen: `WHITE COTTON IN A VAT.` → `SAFFRON, INDIGO, DEEP RED.` → `THE COLOR GOES INTO EVERY THREAD.`

segments.voice: Back in the eleventh ashtpadi, Sukhmani called God the doer of all. The fifteenth comes at that thought from another side. Its first stanza says, in paraphrase: nothing happens by a person's own doing, though they long for it a hundred times. Gurbani elsewhere gives that thought a color. Rang means color and dye, but in Punjabi it also means joy, love, mood, the delight of a festival. So being dyed in His rang says more than: God controls everything. It pictures everything soaked in God, the way dyed cloth is soaked in color. Our actions are still ours, the way the cloth is still cloth. Sikhs work hard, study, serve and plan; nobody is told to sit and wait. But in this picture every thread of that doing is already colored by the One Sukhmani calls the Giver, the One full of every power. The strength in the arms, the idea that arrived, the breath that let the sentence finish: none of it, the stanza says, comes by our own doing alone. One version of this picture in Gurbani is a deep red dye from the madder root, majeeth. Cloth dyed with majeeth was said to keep its color through every wash, and hymns ask to be dyed like that, so deeply in the Name that nothing washes it out. So nothing on our own isn't an insult to your effort. It's a description of what your effort is made of. And when the doing is soaked in someone else's color, the natural response, once it's done, is thanks.
screen: `THE DOER OF ALL, ANOTHER SIDE.` · `RANG: COLOR, DYE, JOY, LOVE.` · `STILL CLOTH, BUT SOAKED THROUGH.` · `MAJEETH: THE COLOR THAT STAYS.` · then, large: `IN HIS COLOR.`

segments.voice: Pick something tiny you can do right here, straighten your back, take one slow, full breath, unclench your hands, and do it with attention. Then notice what made it possible, the muscles, the air, the moment of quiet, and let a thank-you rise to whoever or whatever you understand that to be. If you pray, you can say Waheguru at each thank-you.
Rang, color, dye, also joy. Nothing comes by our own doing alone; in Gurbani's picture it is soaked in His rang, like cloth soaked through with dye.
Your line: in his color. Still cloth, soaked through. Four hundred ninety-six days, and counting.

howItsDone: Gurbani often speaks of being dyed in the Name, like cloth in fast madder dye, and Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's fifteenth ashtpadi hear that nothing is done by one's own doing alone.

chat.says: If nothing happens by our own doing, why work hard at all?
options: Our doing is still ours, as dyed cloth is still cloth; Sikhs work hard, soaked in His color.
There's no point; Sukhmani says to sit and wait, since God will do it all without us.
Work hard only at religious tasks; ordinary jobs aren't soaked in His color.
chat.meaning: The stanza says nothing comes by our own doing alone, yet Sikhs work, study and serve: effort stays ours, soaked through like dyed cloth.
